title: "Next.js"
description: "Add Seamless Auth to a Next.js App Router application: serve the /auth routes from a route handler, read the session in server components, and protect pages in proxy.ts."

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'

A Next.js App Router application can be its own Seamless Auth backend. Two packages do the work:

| Package                 | Runs in                                | Gives you                                                                                   |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@seamless-auth/nextjs` | Route handlers, server components, `proxy.ts` | The `/auth` routes, server-side session reads, and route protection                 |
| `@seamless-auth/react`  | Client components                      | `AuthProvider`, `useAuth()`, and the headless client, exactly as in any React app           |

With both, there is no separate API server for auth. The browser calls `/auth` on the
application's own origin, the session cookies stay first-party, and the server can render the
signed-in user on the first paint.

Requires `@seamless-auth/nextjs` 0.2.0 or later and `@seamless-auth/react` 0.14.0 or later
(0.14.0 is the release that made the React SDK safe to render from the App Router).

```txt
browser
  -> your Next.js app: app/auth/[...seamless]/route.ts   (@seamless-auth/nextjs)
  -> Seamless Auth API
```

<Aside type="tip">
  A complete starter with everything on this page wired up lives in
  [`seamless-templates`](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-templates/tree/main/templates/fullstack/nextjs)
  under `templates/fullstack/nextjs`. `seamless init` does not offer it yet, so copy that directory
  and follow its README.
</Aside>

---

## Install

```bash
npm install @seamless-auth/nextjs @seamless-auth/react
```

`react-router-dom` is not needed. It is an optional peer of `@seamless-auth/react`, used only by
the built-in screens, which a Next.js app does not use (see
[Sign-In Screens](#sign-in-screens)).

---

## Step 1: Serve The Auth Routes

Mount a catch-all route handler at `app/auth/[...seamless]/route.ts`:

```ts
import { createSeamlessAuthHandler } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'

export const { GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE } = createSeamlessAuthHandler({
  authServerUrl: process.env.AUTH_SERVER_URL!,
  audience: process.env.AUTH_SERVER_URL!,
  cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY!,
  serviceSecret: process.env.API_SERVICE_TOKEN!,
  jwksKid: process.env.JWKS_KID,
})
```

This serves the same routes and issues the same cookies as `@seamless-auth/express` and
`@seamless-auth/fastify`, for both cookie and bearer transport. Its tests hold it to identical
responses from the Express adapter.

- `cookieSecret` and `serviceSecret` must be at least 32 characters, and `serviceSecret` must
  match the auth API's `API_SERVICE_TOKEN`. Both are checked when the handler is created.
- The handler signs cookies with `jsonwebtoken`, so it needs the Node.js runtime, which is the
  default. Do not set `export const runtime = 'edge'`.

<Aside type="caution">
  `next build` imports route modules with no request and often no secrets. If your build
  environment has no `.env`, create the handler on the first request instead of at module scope,
  or the secret check fails the build. The starter does this with a small lazy wrapper.
</Aside>

### Options

`createSeamlessAuthHandler` takes the same options as the Express and Fastify adapters, plus
`basePath`:

| Option                   | Default                        | Purpose                                                   |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `authServerUrl`          | required                       | Base URL of your Seamless Auth instance                   |
| `audience`               | required                       | Audience your user tokens are issued for                  |
| `cookieSecret`           | required                       | Signs the session cookies, 32 characters minimum          |
| `serviceSecret`          | required                       | Shared secret for machine-to-machine calls                |
| `jwksKid`                | `dev-main`                     | `kid` header on the HS256 service tokens the adapter signs for the auth API; not the API's signing key ID. Warns while unset or `dev-main` |
| `basePath`               | `/auth`                        | Where the catch-all route is mounted                      |
| `cookieDomain`           | none                           | Domain attribute for the auth cookies                     |
| `cookieSecure`           | `true`                         | Set `false` only for local HTTP development               |
| `cookieSameSite`         | `none` when secure, else `lax` | SameSite policy                                           |
| `allowedOrigins`         | none                           | Origin allowlist for browsers without `Sec-Fetch-Site`    |
| `accessCookieName`       | `seamless-access`              | Session cookie name                                       |
| `registrationCookieName` | `seamless-ephemeral`           | Registration cookie name                                  |
| `refreshCookieName`      | `seamless-refresh`             | Refresh cookie name                                       |
| `preAuthCookieName`      | `seamless-ephemeral`           | Login-initiation cookie name                              |
| `messaging`              | none                           | Your own email and SMS delivery for codes and magic links |
| `resolveClientIp`        | none                           | Picks the end user's IP to forward to the auth API        |

**Client IP.** A route handler has no trustworthy source for the client address, because any
caller can set `X-Forwarded-For`. Nothing is forwarded unless you pass `resolveClientIp` and read
the header your platform sets and a client cannot, for example `x-real-ip` on Vercel. A value that
is not an IP address is dropped. The browser's `User-Agent` is always forwarded, capped at 512
characters.

Two behaviors differ from Express because a route handler has no framework underneath: request
bodies are parsed here, exactly as Express's `json()` does (only `application/json`, strict,
100kb maximum), and an unknown route answers `404 { "error": "not_found" }` as JSON.

## Step 2: Add The Provider

Every module in `@seamless-auth/react` is a client component, so `AuthProvider` can be rendered
straight from the root layout. Pass the session the server resolved as `initialSession`:

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import { cookies, headers } from 'next/headers'
import { getSeamlessSession } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'
import { AuthProvider } from '@seamless-auth/react'

export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'

export default async function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const session = await getSeamlessSession(await cookies(), {
    authServerUrl: process.env.AUTH_SERVER_URL!,
    cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY!,
    serviceSecret: process.env.API_SERVICE_TOKEN!,
    jwksKid: process.env.JWKS_KID,
    userAgent: (await headers()).get('user-agent') ?? undefined,
  })

  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <AuthProvider apiHost="" initialSession={session}>
          {children}
        </AuthProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

- **`apiHost=""`** sends every auth request to `/auth` on the page's own origin, which is the
  route handler from step 1.
- **`initialSession`** makes the first paint render the signed-in user instead of a loading state.
  The provider then revalidates in the background, without reporting `loading`, which fills in
  anything the server did not have and signs out a session that was revoked. It is read once,
  when the provider creates its session.
- **Hydration is safe.** The first client render matches the server's: `hasSignedInBefore` is
  `false` on both and turns `true` straight after hydration when the browser remembers a sign-in.
- **Props from a server component must be serializable.** `apiHost`, `magicLinkRedirectUri`, and
  `initialSession` are. `transport` and `ports` take functions, so set those from a client
  component that wraps the provider.

### How `getSeamlessSession` reads the session

It verifies the access cookie locally, then asks the auth API for `/users/me` with the token
inside it. The result is the `/users/me` wire type, the same one `initialSession` takes, so it
passes straight through.

It **never refreshes**. When the access cookie has expired it returns `null`, even if the refresh
cookie is still valid. A refresh from the server would rotate the refresh token in a response the
browser never receives, and the browser's own next refresh would then be refused as a replay,
which revokes the session. Returning `null` costs nothing: the provider's background revalidation
renews the session through `/auth` straight after the page loads.

<Aside type="danger">
  For the same reason, never call your own `/auth/users/me` from server code with the browser's
  cookies forwarded. When the access cookie has expired, the adapter refreshes inside that request
  and the browser loses the session.
</Aside>

Server code that needs helpers or types (`hasScopedRole`, `roleGrantsAccess`, `User`) imports them
from `@seamless-auth/nextjs` or `@seamless-auth/client`, never from `@seamless-auth/react`.
Everything exported from `@seamless-auth/react` is a client reference inside a server component,
including the pure helpers.

---

## Step 3: Protect Pages In `proxy.ts`

```ts
// proxy.ts
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server'
import { hasSeamlessSession } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'

export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  if (hasSeamlessSession(request.cookies, { cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY! })) {
    return NextResponse.next()
  }

  const login = new URL('/login', request.url)
  login.searchParams.set('next', `${request.nextUrl.pathname}${request.nextUrl.search}`)
  return NextResponse.redirect(login)
}

export const config = { matcher: ['/dashboard/:path*'] }
```

`hasSeamlessSession` checks the cookies locally, with no network call. A valid refresh cookie
counts as a session, because its access cookie may only have expired and the next call to `/auth`
renews it. Treating that as signed out would send a returning user to the sign-in page once every
access-token lifetime.

`proxy.ts` is the Next.js 16 name and runs on the Node.js runtime. On Next.js 15.5 or later, use
`middleware.ts` with `export const config = { runtime: 'nodejs' }`. The Edge runtime cannot verify
the cookies.

For a role check, `getSeamlessClaims` returns what the access cookie says about the user, also
locally:

```ts
import { getSeamlessClaims, hasScopedRole } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'

const claims = getSeamlessClaims(request.cookies, { cookieSecret })

if (!claims || !hasScopedRole(claims.roles, 'admin:read')) {
  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/', request.url))
}
```

The claims leave out the upstream access token, so they are safe to pass to a client component.
Treat them as a routing hint; enforce authorization again in the route handlers that serve data.

### Your own API routes

An application route handler checks the session the same way:

```ts
// app/api/reports/route.ts
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { getSeamlessClaims, hasScopedRole } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'

export async function GET() {
  const claims = getSeamlessClaims(await cookies(), { cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY! })

  if (!claims) return Response.json({ error: 'unauthenticated' }, { status: 401 })
  if (!hasScopedRole(claims.roles, 'reports:read')) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'forbidden' }, { status: 403 })
  }

  return Response.json(await loadReports(claims.id))
}
```

From a client component, call it with `useAuthorizedFetch()`, which sends the session cookies.

## Sign-In Screens

`AuthRoutes`, the React SDK's built-in screens, routes with react-router, which a Next.js app does
not have. Build the screens with the hooks instead: `useAuth()`, `useAuthClient()`, and
`usePasskeySupport()`. [How To Build Your Own Auth UI](/build/custom-auth-ui) covers the flows.
Points that matter in practice:

- **Email codes are six letters, SMS codes are six digits.** A code field that keeps only digits
  rejects every emailed code. Match the input to the channel.
- **Magic links land on `/verify-magiclink`.** The auth API builds the emailed link to that path,
  so serve a page there that calls `verifyMagicLink(token)`. Verifying does not sign in the tab
  that opened the link: the session belongs to the browser that asked for it, which collects it
  from `checkMagicLink()`. When the link is opened in that same browser, calling
  `checkMagicLink()` and then `refreshSession({ background: true })` signs this tab in too.
  Otherwise, tell the reader to return to the device that asked.
- **A magic link is single use, and Strict Mode runs effects twice in development.** Keep the
  verification request in a ref so a remount reuses it instead of sending the token again.
- **A `429` means slow down.** The auth server rate-limits code sends and checks. Read
  `error.status` on the result and say so, instead of reporting a wrong code.

The starter's `src/components/SignIn.tsx` and `src/components/VerifyMagicLink.tsx` implement all of
this.

---

## Deploying

- Run the app on the Node.js runtime with the environment variables above set at runtime.
- `output: 'standalone'` in `next.config.ts` produces a self-contained server; the starter's
  `Dockerfile` packages it on port 80 with a `/health` route.
- Add the application's origin to the auth server's `ORIGINS` so passkey ceremonies verify.
